ai.definition: Stellar Engineering is a theoretical and speculative field that explores the manipulation of stars to harness their energy as a potential sustainable solution.
ai.howItWorks: Theoretical concepts include manipulating stellar fusion and fission processes, though no practical methods or technologies currently exist. It involves advanced astrophysics and materials science to understand and potentially control these phenomena.
ai.problemSolved: Addressing the global need for clean, virtually limitless energy sources by tapping into the power of stars.
ai.manufacturing: None at current stage; purely theoretical.
ai.costDrivers: Unknown due to speculative nature; would involve cutting-edge research and development in astrophysics and materials science, as well as potentially complex engineering challenges.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Long-term theoretical exploration with no known path to practical implementation or commercialization at present.
ai.regulation: None applicable due to speculative nature; would require new frameworks if developed further.
ai.risks: High, including scientific uncertainty, ethical concerns, and potential environmental impacts of manipulating stellar processes.
ai.profitability: Not applicable in current stage; purely theoretical with no economic or commercial value.
ai.futureDevelopment: Potential for significant breakthroughs in understanding stellar physics but unlikely to be economically viable or practical in the near future.

glossary.def: The process by which stars generate energy through nuclear reactions, combining lighter atomic nuclei into heavier ones.
A hypothetical concept involving the splitting of stellar matter, though not currently understood or possible with current technology.

subsystems.name: Collector swarm
subsystems.role: vast numbers of independent solar-collecting satellites orbiting the star, rather than one solid shell.

subsystems.name: Material supply chain
subsystems.role: supplies the raw mass — a swarm large enough to matter would require dismantling planets or moons.

subsystems.name: In-space manufacturing
subsystems.role: builds collectors where the material is, instead of launching them from a planet.

subsystems.name: Power transport
subsystems.role: moves collected energy to where it is used, across interplanetary distances.

subsystems.name: Star-lifting system
subsystems.role: extracts plasma directly from the star to alter its mass, spin or fusion rate.

subsystems.name: Thermal and control layer
subsystems.role: any structure absorbing stellar output must re-radiate waste heat, which is how such objects would be detected.

buildSteps.title: Characterise the star
buildSteps.detail: Measure mass, rotation, magnetic activity and internal structure using helioseismology so any intervention can be modelled.

buildSteps.title: Prove autonomous off-world manufacturing
buildSteps.detail: Demonstrate machines that mine, refine and build copies of themselves from asteroid material with little or no Earth resupply.

buildSteps.title: Dismantle a small body
buildSteps.detail: Start with a moon or asteroid, processing its mass into structural stock — a single planet like Mercury holds roughly 3×10²³ kg of usable material.

buildSteps.title: Deploy a first ring
buildSteps.detail: Place a small number of collectors in a stable orbit, test beamed power transmission and station-keeping.

buildSteps.title: Grow the swarm
buildSteps.detail: Add collectors until a measurable fraction of the star's output — for the Sun about 3.8×10²⁶ W — is intercepted.

buildSteps.title: Scale to a partial shell
buildSteps.detail: Over centuries, build up many overlapping orbital bands until the star's visible light is largely converted to infrared waste heat.

buildSteps.title: Begin star lifting
buildSteps.detail: Use magnetic fields to draw plasma off the surface, controlling the star's mass and fusion rate and extending its lifetime.

buildSteps.title: Operate and evolve the star
buildSteps.detail: Steady-state management: feed or remove material, steer the star's motion with asymmetric radiation, and route power to the civilisation using it.

prerequisites.why: a swarm of this scale cannot be launched from a planet; it must build itself.
robotic sample handling and small-scale resource experiments exist, but nothing at industrial scale.
space stations are assembled in orbit, but nothing approaching megastructure scale.
microwave and laser power transfer have been demonstrated over kilometres, not interplanetary distances.
tokamaks confine grams of plasma; this would require controlling a star.

pathway.milestone: robotic asteroid and lunar resource missions
pathway.unlocks: the beginnings of a material supply chain off Earth.

pathway.milestone: self-sustaining orbital factories and large solar power satellites
pathway.unlocks: building energy infrastructure in space without launching every kilogram from the ground.

pathway.milestone: a small, deliberately built collector swarm
pathway.unlocks: a detectable, scalable energy source independent of any planet.

pathway.milestone: partial stellar capture and the first star-lifting experiments
pathway.unlocks: control over a star's output and lifespan.

pathway.milestone: full stellar management, including moving a star
pathway.unlocks: energy and mobility on a scale no planetary civilisation can reach.
